::: {.why}
Every instinct you have about model capacity, feature count and validation was calibrated on problems where the explainable variance is percent rather than tenths of a percent, and recalibrating that is the whole point of this week.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- State the out-of-sample R-squared you should expect on daily cross-sectional equity returns, and convert it to an information coefficient.
- Say how many observations you need to distinguish an R-squared of 0.002 from zero, and compare against your sample.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>65 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [30 min]{.task-min} Convert between the units you will see in papers and the ones you use: an information coefficient of 0.03 corresponds to an R-squared of about 0.0009 in a cross-sectional regression, and both correspond to a specific information ratio at your breadth. Write the three conversions out and check them numerically on one of your existing signals.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [25 min]{.task-min} Read the results section of Gu, Kelly and Xiu and find the out-of-sample R-squared numbers they report. Note the magnitude, note that they are positive and economically meaningful, and note that a model with that R-squared would be discarded immediately in any other field you have worked in.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [10 min]{.task-min} Compute the sample size question: at your universe size and sample length, what is the standard error of an out-of-sample R-squared of 0.002? Write the number where you will see it every time you are tempted by a model comparison.
:::
:::

## Resources

- [Gu, Kelly & Xiu (2020) — Empirical Asset Pricing via Machine Learning](https://dachxiu.chicagobooth.edu/download/ML.pdf) [paper]{.res-kind}
